To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1. Al is toxic to the kidney of rats, but an adequate dietary intake of calcium may protect the renal tubule cells from Al toxicity; 2. Cd-MT may be more toxic to the renal tubules than CdCl2 and this may be explained by the fact that Cd-MT is taken up by the kidney more readily than CdCl2;
the effects of aluminium and cadmium on kidney function and histological structure are more severe in rats with low calcium intake.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of aluminium (Al) on the renal function of rats.
the effects of Al and/or Cd-MT on the kidney function of rats.
the effects of exposure to aluminum and/or cadmium in rats on creatinine excretion, and concentrations of selected essential metals in kidney and urine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the administration of Cd-MT and/or AlCl3 to rats resulted in a decreased rate of creatinine excretion, and that the renal damage induced by Al was prevented by an adequate calcium intake.
the nephrotoxicity of Al and Cd-MTs in rats was not additive but synergistic.
Al is toxic to the kidney of rats, but the toxicity of Al can be reduced by an adequate supply of Ca in the diet.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the toxic effects of Al and Cd are potentiated by a deficiency of Ca in food.
Al and/or Cd-MT induced renal tubule damage, which was more pronounced in rats with calcium-deficient diet.
Al and Cd-MTs are nephrotoxic and that an adequate supply of Ca protects to some extent the kidney tubules from Al-induced tubule damage.
